Bond purchase cash: separate the clean quote, accrued interest and next coupon

Reconcile an original coupon-bond purchase, distinguish full coupon cash from the holding-period result and trace the transfer from bond value to cash in four interactive figures.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile an invented coupon-bond settlement with the next coupon and a sale

Interactive planning lab

Cash required for dirty purchase price plus the separate fee$9,960
Full next coupon assumed received in cash$200
Net cash result after that coupon and the assumed sale$80

Original coupon-bond cash illustration. Annual coupon cash is split into two equal payments. The single coupon period has an invented 180-day denominator, with straight-line accrued coupon from day zero; it is not an Actual/Actual, Actual/365 or 30/360 market-convention calculation. The entered day is the settlement observation, not a trade-date settlement-rule calculation. The buyer is assumed entitled to the entire next coupon, paid in full on day 180, and sells the still-outstanding bond immediately afterward at the selected clean price. There is no maturity principal repayment. The quote path between those two selected prices is a linear teaching assumption, not a yield-based bond valuation or market forecast. Fees are separate cash charges. Embedded spreads, markdowns, default, ex-coupon trading, taxes, reinvestment, withholding and settlement delays are not calculated. The valuation chart excludes fees; both fees enter the final cash reconciliation exactly once. 90 model days remain until the coupon. Results are holding-period dollars, not yield to maturity, an annualized return or a product recommendation.

The central idea

A clean quote excludes accrued coupon. Include it and separate charges in settlement cash, then reconcile the next coupon with what was already paid before calling the receipt investment profit.

01

A quoted clean price is one component of the cash requirement

A coupon bond can be quoted at a price that excludes interest accrued since its preceding coupon date. A purchase cash requirement can therefore exceed the amount obtained by simply multiplying that quote by the face holding.

ICE’s clean-price definition distinguishes the price without accrued interest from the dirty price. Its accrued-interest reference connects the accumulated amount to the part of the coupon period already elapsed. The definitions describe the components; the numerical illustration here is independently authored.

The example assumes CAD 10,000 face amount and an executed clean quote of 98.5 per CAD 100 face. Clean purchase value is therefore CAD 9,850. That is different from the CAD 10,000 contractual face amount and from the total cash needed to complete this purchase.

The bond remains outstanding after the next coupon. The example sells it then; it does not redeem at maturity or receive face value as an additional payment.

02

State the coupon and day-count assumptions explicitly

The annual coupon rate is 4% of face, paid in two equal instalments. Each coupon is CAD 10,000 × 4% ÷ 2 = CAD 200. One chosen coupon period contains 180 model days.

Settlement occurs after ninety completed days, halfway through that period. Straight-line accrued coupon is CAD 200 × 90 ÷ 180, or CAD 100. Dirty purchase value is clean value plus that amount: CAD 9,850 + CAD 100 = CAD 9,950.

A separate CAD 10 purchase charge makes the total cash requirement CAD 9,960. The fee is not accrued interest, and the accrued interest is not a second fee.

The 180-day denominator is a teaching assumption. It does not implement an actual bond’s calendar, coupon entitlement, settlement rule or day-count convention. The entered elapsed day refers to the settlement observation. Actual transactions require the instrument’s confirmed dates, conventions and entitled coupon.

03

Receiving the full coupon does not mean earning it all after purchase

The buyer is assumed entitled to the full CAD 200 coupon paid on day 180. However, CAD 100 of accrued coupon was already included in the purchase price ninety model days earlier.

Subtracting that purchased accrued amount leaves a CAD 100 holding-period coupon component before fees or changes in the clean price. Calling the entire CAD 200 receipt new profit would omit part of the initial outlay.

Investor.gov’s accrued-interest glossary describes interest accumulated before payment. Cash payment and the period associated with that amount are therefore separate records. This article’s subtraction is a cash-result reconciliation, not an assessment of taxable interest or any available deduction.

Nearness to the coupon date does not make the full coupon a windfall under this model. At day 179, approximately CAD 198.89 of the CAD 200 coupon is already in purchased accrual. Only about CAD 1.11 remains in the holding-period coupon component before fees and price changes.

04

Watch the coupon move from bond value to cash

With the default unchanged clean quote, bond value immediately before the coupon is CAD 9,850 plus the full CAD 200 accrued coupon, or CAD 10,050. Immediately after payment, accrued coupon resets to zero in the illustration and bond value is CAD 9,850.

The buyer now holds CAD 200 of coupon cash alongside that CAD 9,850 bond value. Combined resources remain CAD 10,050 across the payment event. Adding the coupon to the pre-payment CAD 10,050 bond value would count the distributed amount twice.

The change chart subtracts opening dirty value, CAD 9,950, from the bond-value observations. Before payment, the bond change is +CAD 100. After payment, it is −CAD 100, accompanied by CAD 200 cash. The combined change stays +CAD 100 across those two observations.

Showing changes makes this transfer visible beside a larger face holding. The chart ends before the sale and excludes both fees. Between the chosen purchase and sale quotes, the clean-value path is assumed linear; it is not a bond-pricing model or a forecast.

05

Reconcile actual assumed receipts against the complete purchase outlay

Immediately after the next coupon, the default assumed clean sale quote is still 98.5. Gross sale value is CAD 9,850. Subtracting a separate CAD 10 sale charge leaves CAD 9,840 of sale cash.

Sale cash plus the CAD 200 coupon is CAD 10,040. Subtract the original CAD 9,960 purchase cash and the net result is CAD 80, before tax and with every assumed payment completed.

The result waterfall reaches the same answer through components: CAD 200 coupon minus CAD 100 purchased accrued coupon, plus zero clean-price change, minus CAD 10 purchase fee and CAD 10 sale fee.

This second route helps identify omissions. Face principal is already represented by selling the bond and cannot be added again as a redemption. Neither fee is deducted a second time. The coupon percentage alone does not identify the holding-period gain or yield to maturity.

06

Vary the exit quote without treating a coupon as price protection

Change the clean sale quote to 96 while retaining the default purchase and ninety-day settlement. Clean value falls from CAD 9,850 to CAD 9,600, a CAD 250 decrease. The CAD 100 holding-period coupon component less CAD 20 of fees cannot offset that change: the net result is −CAD 170.

Investor.gov’s selling-before-maturity explanation discusses changing sale values and dealing costs. This calculator selects the exit quote directly; it does not derive a price from interest rates, credit changes or a market yield curve.

The signed matrix changes both the settlement day and the later clean quote. A later settlement has a different holding period, so its dollar result cannot be read as an annualized performance ranking against an earlier settlement.

Prices, accrual and charges can all affect the cash result. The matrix assigns no probabilities and does not establish that any displayed trade can be executed.

07

Use the confirmed settlement record for an implemented plan

For a real purchase, identify the face quantity, the quotation convention, settlement date, coupon schedule, day-count basis, accrued amount and separately charged costs. Check whether a quoted execution price already incorporates a dealer markup or markdown before adding a charge again.

The model assumes the promised coupon arrives in full and the buyer can sell immediately afterward at the chosen quote. It does not test creditworthiness, liquidity, settlement delays or ex-coupon arrangements. It also excludes tax, currency conversion and reinvestment.

A dated goal needs the cash amount and the date it becomes usable. A future coupon is different from current settlement cash, and a market value is different from net sale proceeds.

The four figures make those records visible: price components for the purchase, a coupon transfer in the valuation, a complete cash-result bridge and conditional price-and-timing comparisons. Keep them together when reviewing the transaction rather than allowing the next cash receipt to stand in for the whole investment outcome.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts use a chosen 180-day coupon period, selected execution quotes, linear accrual and separate fees. They calculate cash amounts, without a market yield curve, actual day-count convention, annualized return or tax result. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
